statement: If $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert=n$ is such that the subset sums $\sum_{a\in S}a$ are distinct for all $S\subseteq A$ then\[N \gg 2^{n}.\]
solved_note: [db status: disproved; overall: disproved (Lean) (2026-09-03); informal last_update 2025-08-31] This was disproved by GPT-6 Astra (see the proof expositions), which proved that, for any $\epsilon>0$, there are arbitrarily large $n$ such that\[N\leq \epsilon 2^n.\]The trivial lower bound is $N \gg 2^{n}/n$, since all $2^n$ distinct subset sums must lie in $[0,Nn)$. Erdős and Moser [Er56] proved\[ N\geq (\tfrac{1}{4}-o(1))\frac{2^n}{\sqrt{n}}.\](In [Er85c] Erdős offered \$100 for any improvement of the constant $1/4$ here.) A number of improvements of the constant have been given (see [St23] for a history), with the current record $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ first proved in unpublished work of Elkies and Gleason. If $F(x)$ is the size of such a set then this problem is equivalent to\[F(x) <\log_2x+O(1).\]The GPT construction above proves that in fact, for any constant $C>0$, for infinitely many $x$,\[F(x)>\log_2x+C\]for some absolute constant $c>0$. (The second proof of [DFX21] applies also to this generalisation.) This generalisation seems to have first appeared in [Gr71].

statement: Is there a distinct covering system all of whose moduli are odd?
solved_note: [db status: verifiable; overall: verifiable (2025-08-31); informal last_update 2025-08-31] The answer to this stronger question is no, proved by Balister, Bollobás, Morris, Sahasrabudhe, and Tiba [BBMST22]. statement: Let $f(n,k)$ be minimal such that every family $\mathcal{F}$ of $n$-uniform sets with $\lvert \mathcal{F}\rvert \geq f(n,k)$ contains a $k$-sunflower. Is it true that\[f(n,k) < c_k^n\]for some constant $c_k>0$?

Kostochka [Ko97] improved this slightly (in particular establishing an upper bound of $o(n!)$, for which Erdős awarded him the consolation prize of \$100), but the bound stood at $n^{(1+o(1))n}$ for a long time until Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang [ALWZ20] proved\[f(n,k) < (Ck\log n\log\log n)^n\]for some constant $C>1$. This proof was streamlined by Hu. In [Er81] Erdős offered \$1000 for a proof or disproof even just in the special case when $k=3$, which he expected 'contains the whole difficulty'.

A finite projective plane of order $n$ is a collection of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n^2+n+1\}$ of size $n+1$ such that every pair of elements is contained in exactly one set.
solved_note: [db status: falsifiable; overall: falsifiable (2025-08-31); informal last_update 2025-08-31] This conjecture has been proved for $n\leq 11$, but it is open whether there exists a projective plane of order $12$. Bruck and Ryser [BrRy49] have proved that if $n\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ or $n\equiv 2\pmod{4}$ then $n$ must be the sum of two squares.

statement:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be such that $A+A$ has positive (upper) density. Can one always decompose $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ such that $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ both have positive (upper) density?

Is there a basis $A$ of order $2$ such that if $A=A_1\sqcup A_2$ then $A_1+A_1$ and $A_2+A_2$ cannot both hav
solved_note: [db status: solved; overall: solved (Lean) (2025-08-31); informal last_update 2025-08-31] Erdős [Er94b] thought he could construct a basis as in the second question, but 'could never quite finish the proof'. DeepMind and an internal OpenAI model (see the comments and [APSSV26]) have independently constructed a basis which gives an affirmative answer to the second question. statement: Let $C(x)$ count the number of Carmichael numbers in the interval $[1,x]$. Is it true that $C(x)=x^{1-o(1)}$?
solved_note: [db status: open; overall: open (2025-09-28); informal last_update 2025-09-28] Erdős [Er56c] proved\[C(x) < x \exp\left(-c \frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right)\]for some constant $c>0$. Pomerance [Po89] gave a heuristic suggesting that this is the true order of growth, and in fact\[C(x)= x \exp\left(-(1+o(1))\frac{\log x\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}\right).\]Alford, Granville, and Pomerance [AGP94] proved that $C(x)\to \infty$, and in fact $C(x)>x^{2/7}$ for large $x$. The lower bound\[C(x)> x^{0.33336704}\]was proved by Harman [Ha08].
